questions.title: Tuples practice 1
choices: It raises a TypeError, because a tuple cannot be changed
It prints ('small', 'regular', 'large')
It prints ('small', 'medium', 'large') and ignores the change
It raises a syntax error, because tuples use square brackets
questions.explanation: Reading `sizes[1]` is allowed, so the line looks harmless. Assigning to it is not, and Python stops the program with a TypeError. Nothing gets ignored quietly, and nothing gets changed. If you picked the second answer, you were reading `sizes` as a list, which is the exact swap this error exists to catch.

questions.title: Tuples practice 2
choices: int tuple
tuple tuple
int int
tuple int
questions.explanation: The comma is what makes a tuple, not the parentheses. `(7)` has no comma, so the parentheses only group the number, and `a` is a plain int. `b` has the trailing comma, so it really is a one-item tuple. If you answered "tuple tuple", you trusted the parentheses, which is the reasonable guess and the one Python does not share.

questions.title: Trace Tuples
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: You build a tuple with parentheses and commas. Reading from it looks exactly like reading from a list, so if you have seen indexing before, you already know this part. The resulting output is '(3, 5)\n3\n2'.

questions.title: Tuples practice 5
questions.prompt: What happens when you run `point = (3, 5)` then `point[0] = 10`?
choices: It raises a TypeError, because tuples do not support item assignment
point becomes (10, 5)
It silently does nothing
It raises an IndexError
questions.explanation: A tuple is immutable, so `point[0] = 10` raises a TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment. Reading `point[0]` is fine, which is why the assignment looks like it should work. To 'change' a tuple you build a new one and reuse the name, as in `point = (10, 5)`.

questions.title: Tuple assignment error
questions.prompt: A student writes `point[0] = 10` after making `point = (3, 5)`. What should they understand?
choices: Tuple positions cannot be rewritten. Make a new tuple or use a list.
The assignment changes only a temporary copy of the tuple.
The code is fine as long as the tuple has at least two values.
The problem is the zero index, because tuple positions start at one.
questions.explanation: `point[0]` can be read, but assigning into that slot tries to mutate the tuple. Python raises a TypeError because tuples are fixed after creation. If the data must change in place, a list is the better structure; if the data should stay fixed, create a new tuple with the new value.

questions.title: One-item tuple comma
questions.prompt: Which line actually creates a one-item tuple?
choices: `value = (4)` because parentheses always create a tuple.
`value = (4,)` because the comma is what makes the one-item tuple.
`value = tuple(4)` because any value can be wrapped directly.
`value = [4,]` because brackets and parentheses mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: For one item, the comma is the signal Python needs. `(4)` is only the number 4 grouped by parentheses, while `(4,)` is a tuple containing one value. This is easy to miss because multi-item tuples already have commas between the items.

questions.title: Fixed coordinate data
questions.prompt: A coordinate like `(row, column)` will not change after it is created. Which structure fits that job?
choices: A list, because fixed pairs should always be editable.
A dictionary, because every pair must use text keys.
Use a tuple when positions have fixed meanings and should stay together.
A set, because row and column order should be ignored.
questions.explanation: A tuple works well when each position has a stable meaning, such as row first and column second. The fixed shape helps readers know what unpacking or indexing means. If the pair needs named fields or frequent edits, another structure may fit better.

questions.title: When not to use tuples
questions.prompt: A program needs to add and remove names while it runs. What should the student use?
choices: A tuple, then call `append` whenever a name arrives.
A tuple, because immutability makes all nested data immutable too.
A tuple, then assign into indexes to replace old names.
A list, because the collection is meant to change over time.
questions.explanation: Tuples are fixed-size containers. A changing roster needs operations such as append, remove, or item assignment, so a list matches the behavior. Choosing a tuple here turns normal updates into TypeErrors instead of making the code safer.

questions.title: Returning multiple values
questions.prompt: A function needs to return both a minimum score and a maximum score. Which pattern is clean in Python?
choices: Return a tuple such as `(low, high)` and unpack the two values at the call site.
Print both values and make the caller read the screen output.
Store the two values in unrelated global variables.
Return only the first value and recalculate the second later.
questions.explanation: Returning a tuple keeps related results together without adding extra global state. The caller can write `low, high = result` or unpack the return value directly. This is useful when the values belong together but do not need a full class or dictionary.

questions.title: Passing fixed inputs
questions.prompt: A helper should read a sequence of settings but should not edit it. Which argument shape best communicates that?
choices: Pass a list so the helper can freely rearrange it.
Pass a tuple so accidental item assignment is blocked.
Pass a set so duplicate settings are automatically removed.
Pass a dictionary so indexes become unpredictable.
questions.explanation: A tuple tells readers the sequence is meant to be read as fixed data. Python also prevents direct item assignment, which catches accidental edits early. It does not make nested mutable objects safe, but it does protect the tuple's own positions.
